hook.question: A fitness app keeps your step count for every day of the year. How can it answer “how many steps between day 3 and day 20?” thousands of times without re-adding every time?
paragraphs: The obvious way adds up days 3 to 20 on every question: 18 additions. A longer stretch means more additions, and the same days get added again and again, once per question.

Now suppose the app also writes down, once and in advance, a running total next to each day: all the steps from day 1 up to that day. Then a question only needs the totals around your stretch. Which two would you look at?
hook.aha: Write the running totals down once. The total at the end of the stretch contains everything before it, and the total just before the stretch is exactly the part you don’t want. Subtract it: total through day 20 − total through day 2. Every question costs one subtraction, whether the stretch is 18 days or 18,000.

metaphor: A car’s odometer shows every kilometre the car has ever driven. To know how far one trip went, you don’t replay the trip: read the odometer when it ends, read it when it started, and subtract.
Each reading already contains everything that came before it, so the part you don’t want cancels out. A prefix array is an odometer reading written next to every number.
mentalModel.click: Total up to the end, minus total up to just before the start: everything before the stretch cancels.

glossary.definition: A second array, one cell longer than nums, holding running totals. prefix[i] is the sum of the first i numbers.
The total of everything added so far while you walk along the array. Each prefix cell is one running sum, frozen.
prefix[0] = 0: the total of no numbers at all. It is the extra cell that makes a range starting at index 0 work like every other range.
A question about a stretch of the array, like “what is the sum from index 2 to index 4?”. Written sum(l..r).
l..r includes both nums[l] and nums[r]. That is why the formula reaches for prefix[r + 1], not prefix[r].
Filling the prefix array once, left to right: prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]. It costs one pass.
In Subarray Sum Equals K: the earlier running sum a stretch ending here would have to start from, which is running sum minus k.

mentalModel.definition: A prefix-sum array of nums (length n) has n + 1 cells: prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i], so prefix[i] is the sum of the first i numbers, nums[0..i−1]. For an inclusive range l..r, sum(nums[l..r]) = prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l]. Building it takes O(n) time and O(n) space; each query then takes O(1). The trick works for any operation you can undo, such as sums, counts and XOR, but not for a maximum or minimum. The same idea extends to two dimensions, and combined with a hash map of earlier running sums it counts the stretches that add up to k.

useWhen: You must answer many questions about the sum (or count, or XOR) of a stretch of the same array.
The array stays the same between questions, so the work done up front is never wasted.
The problem says “subarray sums to k”, “divisible by k” or “equal numbers of 0s and 1s”: a stretch’s total is the difference of two running totals.
A nested loop re-adds the same numbers again and again.
notWhen: The array changes between questions. A prefix array goes stale after every update, so you would need a structure built for updates, such as a Fenwick tree.
You need the maximum or minimum of a stretch. Unlike a sum, a maximum can’t be subtracted out.
One window slides over the data once and you only want its best sum. A sliding window does that with O(1) extra space.

quiz.problem: An array of daily step counts never changes. You must answer 50,000 questions, each asking for the total between day l and day r.
quiz.explanation: Many questions on an unchanging array means paying once up front. Build running totals in one pass, then every question is one subtraction.

quiz.problem: Given an array of numbers and a size k, find the largest sum of any k neighbouring numbers. You are asked once.
quiz.explanation: A prefix array would work, but the size is fixed and you only ask once. Sliding a window of size k, adding the new number and dropping the old one, needs no extra array.

quiz.problem: Given an array that may contain negative numbers and a target k, count how many stretches of neighbouring numbers add up to exactly k.
quiz.explanation: Negatives break a sliding window, because adding a number no longer reliably grows the sum. A stretch sums to k when two running sums differ by k, and a hash map counts the earlier ones.

quiz.problem: Given a sorted array, find two numbers that add up to a target.
quiz.explanation: This is about a pair, not a stretch of neighbours. With a sorted array, one pointer at each end can close in on the target using no extra memory.

quiz.problem: In how many different ways can you climb n stairs if you may take 1 or 2 steps at a time?
quiz.explanation: There is no stretch of an array to total up. The ways to reach a stair are built from the ways to reach the two stairs below it, which is dynamic programming.

pseudocode.text: for each position i in nums:

template.time: O(n) to build, O(1) per query
notes: Build once, then q queries cost O(n + q) in total. Re-adding for every query costs up to O(n · q).

Use n + 1 cells with prefix[0] = 0, so prefix[i] means “the sum of the first i numbers”. Then sum(l..r) = prefix[r + 1] − prefix[l] for every query, including l = 0. The shorter version, prefix[i] = sum(0..i), needs a special case for l = 0.
The range is inclusive, so the right-hand cell is prefix[r + 1]. Reaching for prefix[r] is the classic off-by-one.
It works for anything you can undo: sums, counts, XOR. It does not work for max or min, because you can’t subtract a maximum out.
The array must not change. If it does, rebuilding costs O(n) each time, so use a structure built for updates instead.
Sums can outgrow a 32-bit int on big inputs. Check the constraints, and use a 64-bit type (long in Java, long long in C++) when they are large.

examples.title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
examples.problem: Design a class that stores an integer array nums once, then answers many queries sumRange(left, right): the sum of nums[left..right], both ends included.
approach: The array never changes and queries repeat, so do the adding once, in the constructor, and make each query cheap.
Build prefix with one extra cell: prefix[0] = 0 and prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]. Here it is [0, -2, -2, 1, -4, -2, -3].
sumRange(left, right) = prefix[right + 1] − prefix[left]. So sumRange(0, 2) = prefix[3] − prefix[0] = 1 − 0 = 1.
sumRange(2, 5) = prefix[6] − prefix[2] = -3 − (-2) = -1, and sumRange(0, 5) = -3 − 0 = -3. The leading 0 means left = 0 needs no special case.
examples.time: O(n) to build, O(1) per query

examples.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
examples.problem: Given an integer array nums (it may contain negatives) and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.
approach: A stretch ending at i sums to k when the running sum at i − the running sum before the stretch = k. So at each i, ask how many earlier running sums equal running − k.
Keep a map from running sum to how many times it has appeared. Start it with {0: 1}: the empty prefix, so stretches that begin at index 0 are counted.
Running sums are 1, 2, 3. At i = 1 we need 0, seen once, so +1. At i = 2 we need 1, seen once (after i = 0), so +1.
Look up before you store the current running sum, or with k = 0 a stretch could match itself. The answer is 2. Negatives are fine here, which a sliding window can’t promise.

examples.title: Find Pivot Index
examples.problem: Return the leftmost index whose left-side sum equals its right-side sum (the number at the index is in neither side), or -1 if there is none.
approach: Index i is a pivot when the sum of everything to its left equals the sum of everything to its right.
The left sum is a prefix sum. The right sum is total − left − nums[i], so one running left sum is enough and no prefix array is needed.
The total is 28. At i = 3, left = 1 + 7 + 3 = 11 and right = 28 − 11 − 6 = 11. They match, so 3 is the pivot.
Scan from the left and return the first match, or -1. It is the same trick as a range query: a total minus a part gives the other part.

conceptQuiz.question: With the n + 1 convention, what is prefix for nums = [4, 2, 7, 1]?
conceptQuiz.explanation: prefix[0] = 0, then each cell adds the next number: 0, 4, 4 + 2 = 6, 6 + 7 = 13, 13 + 1 = 14. prefix[i] is the sum of the first i numbers.

conceptQuiz.question: With prefix = [0, 4, 6, 13, 14], what is the sum of nums[1..2]?
conceptQuiz.explanation: sum(1..2) = prefix[3] − prefix[1] = 13 − 4 = 9, which is nums[1] + nums[2] = 2 + 7.

conceptQuiz.question: You build a prefix array once and then answer q range-sum queries on n numbers. What is the total time?
options: O(q), because the build is free
O(n · q), because each query may add up to n numbers
O(n + q): O(n) to build, O(1) per query
conceptQuiz.explanation: One pass builds the array (O(n)). After that each query is two lookups and a subtraction (O(1)), so q queries cost O(q) more.

conceptQuiz.question: What does the extra 0 at the front of the prefix array buy us?
options: A query that starts at index 0 needs no special case.
It lets the array hold negative numbers.
It makes the build pass faster.
conceptQuiz.explanation: For l = 0 the formula reads prefix[r + 1] − prefix[0], and prefix[0] is 0. Without the extra cell you would have to write an if for l = 0.

conceptQuiz.question: In Subarray Sum Equals K, why do we put 0 in the map with a count of 1 before the loop starts?
options: So stretches that begin at index 0 are counted: they need the empty prefix, whose sum is 0.
Because a hash map can’t start empty.
conceptQuiz.explanation: If the first i numbers add up to k, then running − k = 0, and the lookup has to find something. The empty prefix is that something.

practice.title: Running Sum of 1d Array
practice.insight: The answer is the prefix array, almost. Each output is the one before it plus the new number.

practice.title: Product of Array Except Self
practice.insight: Everything except nums[i] is the product on its left times the product on its right. Build prefix products instead of prefix sums.

practice.title: Contiguous Array
practice.insight: Count each 0 as -1. Then equal numbers of 0s and 1s means a stretch totals 0, so look for two equal running sums.

practice.title: Continuous Subarray Sum
practice.insight: Two running sums with the same remainder mod k bound a stretch that is a multiple of k. What should the map remember, and how far apart must the two be?

practice.title: Subarray Sums Divisible by K
practice.insight: Count how often each running-sum remainder has appeared. Careful: the remainder of a negative sum can come out negative.

practice.title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
practice.insight: Prefix sums work in two directions. A rectangle is a big rectangle minus two strips, plus the corner you subtracted twice.

practice.title: Matrix Block Sum
practice.insight: Build the 2D prefix once, then every answer cell is one rectangle query. Clamp the rectangle at the edges of the grid.

practice.title: Maximum Sum of 3 Non-Overlapping Subarrays
practice.insight: Prefix sums give every window of length k in O(1). Then, for each middle window, you need the best window to its left and the best to its right.
